title: Extreme heat
summary: Heat of 90°F or more for two to three days. Cool off, drink fluids and watch the insulin.

sources.title: CDC: Managing Insulin in an Emergency

items.text: Learn the signs of heat illness.
**Do not rely on a fan** as your main cooling. Fans do not lower body temperature.
Find local cooling spots, such as libraries and shopping malls, or ask the health department.
Cover windows with drapes or shades, weather-strip doors and windows, and add insulation.
Plan how to keep insulin cool.
**Never leave people or pets in a closed car.**
No air conditioning? **Go to a cooling center** or another air-conditioned place.
Drink plenty of fluids. Wear loose, light-colored clothing. Seek shade and wear a wide-brimmed hat.
Take cool showers or baths. Use the oven less.
Limit hard outdoor work during midday heat.
Check on family members, older adults and neighbors.
Pets: plenty of cool water and shade. Hot pavement can burn their paws.
If heat causes a power outage, follow the Power outage checklist and go to a community location with power if it gets extreme.
Keep insulin out of heat and direct sun, and check blood sugar more often if it has been kept warm.

phases.title: If someone gets sick from the heat

items.text: **Heat stroke is an emergency. Call 911.** Signs: body temperature above 103°F, hot red dry skin, rapid pulse, confusion or fainting.
items.note: Move the person to shade, remove outer clothing, apply cold wet cloths or ice packs to the head, neck, armpits and groin, and raise their feet.

items.text: Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, paleness, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea or fainting.
items.note: Move to a cooler place, remove extra clothing, and sip water or sports drinks. Call a healthcare provider if symptoms get worse or last more than an hour.

items.text: Heat cramps: muscle pains or spasms.
items.note: Move somewhere cooler, loosen clothing and sip electrolyte drinks.
